title: Da Silva Moore v. Publicis Groupe & MSL Group, 287 F.R.D. 182 (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 24, 2012) (Peck, M.J.)
pub: United States District Court, Southern District of New York
author: Andrew J. Peck (U.S. Magistrate Judge)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The opinion accepts task-specific computer-assisted review and materially develops the cluster’s proposition through a concrete, court-supervised human–AI workflow. It specifies iterative expert training, statistical and judgmental sampling, transparency, proportionality and final human review, demonstrating how selective deployment and quality control can make automation defensible without assuming general competence or perfection.
qs: The accuracy of the search processes, both the systems’ functions and the attorney judgments to train the computer, will be tested and quality controlled by both judgmental and statistical sampling.

st.t: Predictive coding: Mature automation still needs transparency
st.an: Da Silva Moore directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: predictive coding can reduce burdensome manual review, but approval is case-specific and depends on proportionality, transparency, lawyer-designed processes, testing and quality control rather than blanket endorsement of a system.
qs: As with keywords or any other technological solution to ediscovery, counsel must design an appropriate process, including use of available technology, with appropriate quality control testing, to review and produce relevant ESI while adhering to Rule 1 and Rule 26(b)(2)(C) proportionality.

st.t: TAR governance: Reduced review retains legal judgment
st.an: Da Silva Moore directly supports the cluster’s proposition: predictive coding can reduce exhaustive human review, but approval is case-specific and lawyers retain responsibility for training, quality control, proportionality and stopping decisions based on verified results.
qs: The technology exists and should be used where appropriate, but it is not a ease of machine replacing humans: it is the process used and the interaction of man and machine that the courts needs to examine.

First, it is unlikely that courts will be able to determine or approve a party’s proposal as to when review and production can stop until the computer-assisted review software has been trained and the results are quality control verified.

mo.t: AI privilege: Legal subject matter is insufficient
E-discovery evidence: Manual review is no gold standard
Filing duties: AI use never displaces inquiry
Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
Legal prediction: Classification cannot guarantee sound advice
Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
Trial procedure: Advance disclosure protects courtroom management

kp.k: Judicial approval is conditional, not universal or vendor-specific
kp.d: Judge Peck describes the opinion as apparently the first judicial approval of computer-assisted review. Approval concerned a case involving over three million documents, parties agreeing to the technology but disputing implementation, comparative advantages over alternatives, proportionality and transparency. It neither compelled initial adoption nor endorsed a vendor or a universally applicable protocol.
qs: This Opinion appears to be the first in which a Court has approved of the use of computer-assisted review.
Nor does this Opinion endorse any vendor
Computer-assisted review now can be considered judicially-approved for use in appropriate cases.

kp.k: Predictive coding reorganizes review around senior lawyers' judgments
kp.d: Peck explains a human-trained relevance classification process in which senior lawyers code seed documents, assess predictions and provide further training, rather than assigning all review to junior staff. In this case, senior attorneys performed the seed-set review. The account describes task reallocation and selective automation, not autonomous replacement of lawyers or measured changes in firm staffing.
qs: Unlike manual review, where the review is done by the most junior staff, computer-assisted coding involves a senior partner (or [small] team) who review and code a “seed set” of documents.
All of this review to create the seed set was done by senior attorneys (not paralegals, staff attorneys or junior associates).
Typically, the senior lawyer (or team) needs to review only a few thousand documents to train the computer.

kp.k: Published studies challenge manual review's claimed superiority
kp.d: Peck relies on external research, rather than completed results from this litigation, to challenge exhaustive manual review as a gold standard. The 2010 Roitblatt, Kershaw and Oot study found two computer systems at least as accurate as human re-review against the original review. Grossman and Cormack's 2011 analysis of TREC Legal Track data reported higher accuracy with much lower effort, including average human review of only 1.9% of documents. The cited authors also cautioned that technology-assisted processes differ.
qs: “[o]n every measure, the performance of the two computer systems was at least as accurate (measured against the original review) as that of human re-review.”
“The technology-assisted reviews require, on average, human review of only 1.9% of the documents, a fifty-fold savings over exhaustive manual review.”
"not all technology-assisted reviews ... are created equal”

kp.k: Human disagreement undermines assumptions of error-free manual review
kp.d: The opinion reports research identifying fatigue and differences in strategic judgment as sources of reviewer inconsistency. Roitblatt, Kershaw and Oot reported human agreement around 70–75%; another Grossman–Cormack study attributed only 5% of reviewer disagreement to borderline relevance issues. These are findings quoted from other studies, not measurements of the reviewers in this case.
qs: The Roitblatt, Kershaw, Oot article noted that "[t]he level of agreement among human reviewers is not strikingly high,” around 70-75%.
with only 5% of reviewer disagreement attributable to borderline or questionable issues as to relevance.

kp.k: Keyword searches require testing and complementary methods
kp.d: Peck criticizes untested keyword selection for both false positives and missed relevant material, while retaining keywords as useful inputs to predictive-coding training. In this case, “training” yielded 165,208 hits and “compensation” 55,602. He also cites Blair and Marón's 1985 study of 40,000 documents and 51 requests: searchers believed they had met a 75% retrieval target, but average recall was 20%.
qs: Searchers believed they met the goals, but their average recall was just 20%.
Keywords have a place in production of ESI
the proposed methodology must be quality control tested to assure accuracy in retrieval and elimination of “false positives.”

kp.k: Transparency makes automated discovery more defensible
kp.d: MSL agreed to share non-privileged training and iterative-review documents, including those coded irrelevant, together with coding for plaintiffs' scrutiny. Disagreements could be addressed through consultation and judicial resolution. Peck identifies this transparency as important to approval and recommends discussing it in future cases, while acknowledging that not all experienced ESI counsel consider this level of disclosure necessary. Confidentiality, privilege and clawback protections remained applicable.
qs: MSL’s transparency in its proposed ESI search protocol made it easier for the Court to approve the use of predictive coding.
This Court highly recommends that counsel in future cases be willing to at least discuss, if not agree to, such transparency in the computer-assisted review process.
All non-privileged documents reviewed by MSL during each round of the iterative process

kp.k: Training and sampling remain subject to continuing challenge
kp.d: The protocol specifies an initial random sample of 2,399 documents, described as a 95% confidence level with an estimation of plus or minus 2%; supplemental review includes 4,000 randomly sampled documents from plaintiffs' keywords. Iterative training uses at least 500 documents per round, generally for seven rounds, with protocol provisions for earlier stabilization and judicial power to require further rounds. A final 2,399-document sample from excluded documents tests quality. These are agreed procedures, not achieved accuracy findings.
qs: The random sample consists of 2,399 documents, which represents a 95% confidence level with a confidence estimation of plus or minus 2%.
MSL will review 4,000 randomly sampled documents from Plaintiffs’ supplemental list of key words to be coded for relevance and issue tags.
Plaintiffs reserve the right, at all times, to challenge the accuracy and reliability of the predictive coding process and the right to apply to the Court for a review of the process.

kp.k: Final production retains human review and privilege screening
kp.d: The protocol uses software to identify and prioritize potentially relevant email, but provides for manual review of documents predicted relevant before production, unless MSL obtains judicial relief. Relevant, non-privileged documents are then produced. The resulting workflow reduces the material requiring human attention without treating machine classifications as sufficient for final disclosure.
qs: At the conclusion of the iterative review process, all document predicted by Axcelerate to be relevant will be manually reviewed for production.
All documents found by MSL’s review to be relevant and non-privileged documents will be promptly produced to Plaintiffs.

kp.k: Proportionality requires results, not predetermined spending caps
kp.d: Peck rejected MSL's proposal to review and produce only the top 40,000 documents, estimated at $200,000 or $5 per document, before knowing what would be omitted. Stopping decisions require trained-system results, quality control, relevance and litigation stakes as well as costs. The attached protocol preserves MSL's ability to seek relief or cost shifting, rather than establishing its proposed ceiling as an unconditional limit.
qs: The Court rejected MSL’s 40,000 documents proposal as a “pig in a poke.”
While cost is a factor under Rule 26(b)(2)(C), it cannot be considered in isolation from the results of the predictive coding process and the amount at issue in the litigation.
One hot document may require the software to be re-trained (or some other search method employed), while several documents that really do not add anything to the case might not matter.

kp.k: Discovery rules demand reasonable process rather than perfection
kp.d: Responding to plaintiffs' objections, Peck distinguishes the complete-and-correct certification for disclosures under Rule 26(g)(1)(A) from discovery responses governed by Rule 26(g)(1)(B). He argues that no search method could justify absolute completeness in a collection exceeding three million emails and grounds approval in the then-applicable proportionality provisions and Rule 1, rather than perfect retrieval.
qs: Rule 26(g)(1)(B) is the provision that applies to discovery responses.
It does not call for certification that the discovery response is “complete,” but rather incorporates the Rule 26(b)(2)(C) proportionality principle.
While this Court recognizes that computer-assisted review is not perfect, the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure do not require perfection.

kp.k: Discovery search differs from expert evidence admissibility
kp.d: Peck rejects plaintiffs' argument that approving the search protocol violates Rule 702 or Daubert. He distinguishes finding emails during discovery from introducing expert testimony or scientific results at trial; admissibility of individual emails depends on the emails themselves, not the discovery method.
qs: Rule 702 and _Daubert_ simply are not applicable to how documents are searched for and found in discovery.
If MSL sought to have its expert testify at trial and introduce the results of its ESI protocol into evidence, _Daubert_ and Rule 702 would apply.

kp.k: Phased discovery and technical collaboration support cost control
kp.d: Peck recommends beginning with likely relevant custodians and sources while preserving subsequent discovery, extending deadlines where necessary. He urges lawyers to use clients' knowledge of records and terminology and finds participation by vendors, IT personnel or in-house ediscovery counsel helpful in resolving technical disputes. These are practical recommendations for coordinating legal and technical expertise, not findings about new provider market shares.
qs: Second, staging of discovery by starting with the most likely to be relevant sources (including custodians), without prejudice to the requesting party seeking more after conclusion of that first stage review, is a way to control discovery costs.
Fourth, the Court found it very helpful that the parties’ ediscovery vendors were present and spoke at the court hearings where the ESI Protocol was discussed.
It also is important for the vendors and/or knowledgeable counsel to be able to explain complicated ediscovery concepts in ways that make it easily understandable to judges who may not be tech-sawy.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Judge Andrew J. Peck recognises predictive coding as an acceptable discovery search method in appropriate cases and argues that it can reduce document-review costs while improving on manual review and keyword searching.
pts.d: In this February 2012 opinion, Peck approves the use of computer-assisted review in the particular litigation, rather than ordering unwilling parties to adopt it or endorsing a vendor. He argues that large-scale linear manual review is too expensive and that manual review is not a uniquely accurate 'gold standard'. The technology described is human-trained document classification, not generative AI or autonomous legal practice. It shifts part of the work from exhaustive junior-level review to senior-lawyer training, iterative correction and quality control, with software ranking or classifying the remaining documents. The attached protocol still provides for manual review of documents predicted relevant before production, subject to applications for court relief. Peck also presents judicial acceptance as removing a perceived barrier to adoption. His discussion distinguishes discovery search methods from expert evidence offered at trial: he concludes that Rule 702 and Daubert do not govern how documents are found in discovery, while noting that their application could arise if an expert sought to introduce protocol results at trial.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Peck supports his position with published comparative studies, discovery-search research, the case's document volumes and proposed costs, and procedural authority; he does not report completed performance results from this case.
pts.d: Peck cites Roitblatt, Kershaw and Oot's 2010 empirical comparison as finding two computer systems at least as accurate as human re-review when measured against the original review. He cites Grossman and Cormack's 2011 analysis of TREC Legal Track data as finding more accurate technology-assisted review with much less human review; the reported average of 1.9% of documents reviewed and fifty-fold savings are findings from that cited research, not measured savings in Da Silva Moore. He also cites Blair and Maron's 1985 retrieval study, reporting average recall of 20% despite searchers believing they had achieved the requested 75%, and discusses research on human-review disagreement. Case-specific support includes over three million emails and large keyword hit counts, illustrating the burden of manual review without establishing the eventual predictive-coding results. MSL's proposed $200,000 review budget for 40,000 documents was an estimate and proposed limit, not a demonstrated saving or an accepted unconditional cap. Peck grounds permissibility in Rules 1 and 26(b)(2)(C), cooperation and the transparent protocol. Plaintiffs' vendor supported the technology generally but reserved judgment about this implementation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The opinion concerns an available technology in 2012, with case-specific, conditional approval rather than a prediction of universal adoption or guaranteed results.
pts.d: Peck identifies the opinion as apparently the first judicial approval of computer-assisted review and encourages its consideration in future large-data-volume cases without specifying an adoption timetable. Approval here rests on party agreement to use the technology, document volume, comparative advantages, proportionality, cost effectiveness and transparency. The parties disputed implementation, and plaintiffs preserved objections to the protocol. The planned process includes an initial 2,399-document random sample, iterative training and a further 2,399-document sample of excluded documents. The stated 95% confidence level and plus-or-minus-two-percent sampling specification are protocol parameters, not achieved accuracy figures. Seven training rounds were not an absolute ceiling: Peck contemplated further rounds if the system failed to stabilise. Stopping decisions depend on actual results, costs, case scope and the significance of missed documents; discovery need not be perfect, but cost alone does not justify excluding important evidence. No particular vendor, tool or exact protocol is endorsed for all cases.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are litigants in document-intensive cases, their review lawyers, opposing counsel, discovery specialists and supervising courts.
pts.d: Producing parties, and potentially both sides, may save significant legal fees on document review. Senior lawyers take responsibility for seed-set coding and iterative training instead of relying entirely on junior staff to review the full collection. Peck does not quantify job losses or predict a profession-wide staffing transformation. Under this protocol, requesting counsel gain access to non-privileged training and quality-control documents, including documents classified irrelevant, but must review coding, identify disagreements and participate in dispute resolution. Courts assess process defensibility, proportionality and quality-control results rather than demanding perfect retrieval. E-discovery vendors, in-house IT personnel and in-house e-discovery counsel help explain and implement the methods. The source concerns litigation discovery costs and effectiveness, not an explicit claim about closing the civil justice gap.
